```{r setup, include=FALSE}

library(tidyverse)
```

```{r}
strava_runs <- read_csv("data/strava_runs.csv")
```

```{r}
data_5k_10k <- strava_runs %>%
  mutate(
    event = case_when(
      distance..m. > 4998 & distance..m. < 5015  ~ "5k",
      distance..m. > 9998 & distance..m. < 10015 ~ "10k",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(event))
```


## Exercise 1

When you fill the missing part, remove the # symbol before running the code chunk and eval=FALSE

```{r ex1a, out.width="80%", eval=FALSE}
data_5k_10k %>% 
  filter(gender=="M") %>%
  filter(!is.na(average.heart.rate..bpm.)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = average.heart.rate..bpm.)) + 
  geom_histogram(bins = 20)
```

Histogram shape: high in the middle and low on both sides, it's approximately normally diatributed, because mean = 147.9444	 , median = 147.9.
Distribution characteristics: the average running heart rate of male students is mainly concentrated between 137.5 bpm and 162.5 bpm.

## Exercise 2

```{r ex2, out.width = "80%"}
# Write your code to answer exercise 2a here
data_5k_10k %>%
 mutate(pace_min_per_km=elapsed.time..s./60/(distance..m./1000)) %>% filter(!is.na(pace_min_per_km)) %>% filter(!is.na(gender)) %>%    ggplot(mapping=aes(x=event,y=pace_min_per_km))+     geom_boxplot()+facet_wrap(~gender,nrow=1)+
labs(title="Pace(min/km) comparison for 5k and 10k runs,by gebder", x="Race distance",y="Pace(min/km)")


```


Regardless of gender, the pace for running 10 km is always greater than for 5 km; for the same distance, men's pace is faster than women's.

## Exercise 3

```{r ex3, out.width = "80%"}
# Write your code to answer exercise 3 here

plot_data <- strava_runs %>%
   mutate(speed = distance..m. / elapsed.time..s.) %>%
  group_by(athlete) %>%
  mutate(avg_distance_km = mean(distance..m. / 1000, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    runner_group = case_when(
      avg_distance_km > 13 ~ "Long-distance runners",
      avg_distance_km < 7  ~ "Short-distance runners",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(runner_group),
         !is.na(speed),
         !is.na(distance..m.)) %>%
  mutate(distance_km = distance..m. / 1000)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = distance_km, y = speed, colour = runner_group)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "Long-distance runners"  = "orange",
    "Short-distance runners" = "forestgreen"))+
    
 
    
  labs(title="Speed vs Distance for Long- and Short-Distance Runners", subtitle="Grouped by runners' average distance: >13 km vs <7 km",
    x = "Run distance (km)",
    y = "Run average speed (m/s)",
    colour = "Runner group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()+ theme(legend.position = "bottom",legend.background = element_blank(),
    legend.key = element_blank(),legend.text = element_text(size = 11),legend.title = element_blank(),legend.key.width = unit(1.5, "cm"))+
    guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1)))


```




Based on the generated scatter plot, the hypothesis is supported: the paces of long-distance and short-distance runners are indeed different. The orange points (long-distance runners) are generally positioned higher (faster speed) and extend to the right (longer distance), while the green points (short-distance runners) are positioned lower (slower speed) and clustered to the left (shorter distance).
## Exercise 4

```{r ex4, out.width = "80%"}
# Write your code to answer exercise 4 here

summary_data <- strava_runs %>%
  filter(!is.na(gender)) %>%  # 移除性别缺失值
  group_by(gender) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_distance_km = mean(distance..m. / 1000, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_elapsed_min = mean(elapsed.time..s. / 60, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
plot_data <- summary_data %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(mean_distance_km, mean_elapsed_min),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  ) %>%
  
mutate(
    metric = factor(metric, 
                    levels = c("mean_distance_km", "mean_elapsed_min"),
                    labels = c("Mean Distance (km)", "Mean Elapsed Time (mins)"))
  )
ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = gender, y = value, fill = gender)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ metric, scales = "free_y") +labs(
    x = "Gender",
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Gender"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    strip.text = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"))


```




The faceted bar charts reveal a clear gender difference in running habits. Male runners exhibit higher average values in both metrics: they run longer distances and spend more elapsed time per activity compared to female runners. The increase in elapsed time is consistent with the greater distance covered, reflecting that males generally log longer, more time-consuming runs in this dataset.
